title: My other half: the self that fell in two
hookLine: the lonely self makes itself fall in two, and the two halves chase each other through every kind of creature
carry: one self fell in two: you are the half
tomorrow: the self is dearer than a son
last: I AM, BEFORE THE EGO ADDS A NAME.

cards: People still say it at weddings: my other half. It sounds like a greeting card. In the Brihadaranyaka, one of the oldest Upanishads, it isn't a greeting card at all.
It's a creation story. The self was alone, and lonely. It wanted a second, and there was no second anywhere.
So it did the only thing it could. It used itself.

teach.h: IT MADE ITSELF FALL IN TWO.
teach.b: The self, the text says, was as big as a man and a woman holding each other. It made itself fall in two, and from that came husband and wife.
The Sanskrit plays on its own words here: the verb for fall is pat, and husband and wife are pati and patni.
Then the text quotes the sage Yajnavalkya, whom we'll meet properly in two days: each of us, he used to say, is like half of something split.
Translators argue over the exact object, half a shell or half a split pea, but the picture is the same. You are the half, and the empty space beside you is the shape of the other.
The two halves joined, and humans were born. Then the story turns strange and wide. She thinks: he made me from himself; how can he join with me?
I'll hide. She becomes a cow; he becomes a bull. She becomes a mare; he, a stallion.
A she-goat, a goat. A ewe, a ram.

teach.h: SHE HIDES; HE FOLLOWS, DOWN TO THE ANTS.
teach.b: And on and on, the text says, down to the ants. Every pair of creatures in the world comes out of that chase. At the end the self knows: I am this whole creation, because I poured it out of myself.
So the story is about a marriage, and about much more.
Here's the Hindu teaching inside it: the one became the many. Everything that comes in twos, wanting and wanted, is the one self looking for itself.
It's part of why Hindu weddings call the wife ardhangini, half of the body, and why Hindu art shows Shiva and Parvati as one figure, half and half, Ardhanarishvara. Neither half is whole alone.

how: Students read this as part of the Brihadaranyaka's creation account in chapter one; in many Hindu weddings the couple is spoken of as two halves of one, and the wife is called ardhangini, the half of the body.

o: a married woman's role in the household
a sacred thread worn by a married man
half: each of us, half of something split

games.q: the split self — tap the pairs.
p: to fall: the self made itself fall
she hid; he became a bull
how far down the pairs go

s: the text says each of us is like half of something split
the story stops with the first human couple
she hides as a cow, he follows as a bull, and so on down to the ants.
the self needed something outside itself to make a second
there was nothing else. it made itself fall in two.

games.q: you are the first woman in the story. you think: he made me from himself, how can he join with me? so you hide as a cow. what does he do?
o: he makes a new companion from himself.
games.why: he becomes a bull. then she's a mare and he a stallion, she a she-goat and he a goat, and so on down to the ants: every pair of creatures.

practice: Bring to mind someone who completes something in you: a partner, a friend, a sibling, a child, someone gone.

Notice the space beside you that only they fill, and don't fix or say anything; just let the space be there, and let it be full. If no one comes to mind, rest in the line itself, and notice how much of the world comes in pairs.

wordCard.voice: Ardha, half. In the Brihadaranyaka, the one self falls into two, and every pair of creatures comes from that split; each of us, Yajnavalkya says, is ardha, half of something split.

orig.note: Sanskrit ardha: half. in Hindu weddings a wife is called ardhangini, half the body.

carryVoice: Your line: one self fell in two: you are the half. Tomorrow, a line about love that sounds like a trap. See you then.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.3–5 (the self falls in two; the pairs of creatures; 'I am this creation')
